On this page
Install

Run npm install brewkit in your project folder. Node 20 or later is required. The installer adds a brewkit.config.js file with sensible defaults, so most projects work straight away.

Configure

Open the config file and set your API key and region. Most teams only change the region and the output folder. Every option is listed in the reference, with its default value and an example.

Deploy

Run brewkit deploy to build and upload your site. The first deploy takes about a minute. Later deploys only upload files that changed, so they usually finish in a few seconds.

Troubleshoot

If a deploy fails, run brewkit doctor. It checks your Node version, API key and network, and prints the fix for each problem it finds.

decisions.title: Modal, drawer, popover, tooltip or toast?

start.question: Must the person deal with it before doing anything else?

then.question: Is it a short decision, like confirming a delete?

then.why: It blocks the page on purpose, so keep it to one clear question with two buttons. Esc and Cancel must close it, and focus returns to what opened it.
Longer forms and details fit in a panel that slides in, keeps the page visible behind it, and closes back to where they were.

then.question: Is it only telling them something already happened?

then.why: A short message at the edge that goes away by itself. Add Undo for anything destructive, and never let a toast be the only place important information appears.

then.question: Is it attached to one button or item on the page?
Will they click things inside it?

then.why: Opens on click, can hold links and controls, and closes with Esc or a click outside.
A short label on hover and keyboard focus. Touch screens have no hover, so never put information people need to finish the task only in a tooltip.
Put the message in the page where it applies. It stays until it is resolved and blocks nothing.

decisions.title: Tabs, segmented control, accordion or stepper?

start.question: Must people go through the parts in a fixed order?

then.why: Shows where they are and what is left. Use it for checkout and sign-up, and let people go back without losing what they typed.

then.question: Do people need to see more than one part at once, or is the screen narrow with long content?

then.why: Sections stack and open in place, which suits phones and FAQs. Write headings people can scan while everything is closed.

then.question: Are the options different views of the same data, like List and Grid or Day, Week and Month?

then.why: A compact switch between 2 to 5 views of the same thing. The content stays the same, only how it is shown changes.
Separate panels of related content on one page. Keep labels short, and few enough tabs that they fit without scrolling.

decisions.title: Pagination, infinite scroll or Load more?

start.question: Do people need to find an item again, share their place, or reach the footer?

then.why: Numbered pages give a sense of place and size, work with the Back button, and keep the footer reachable. Best for search results and catalogs.

then.question: Is it a casual feed people scroll without a goal?

then.why: Loads more as they reach the bottom, which suits social and media feeds. Keep their place when they come back, and do not hide important links in a footer they can never reach.
A middle ground: the list grows only when they ask, so they stay in control and the footer stays reachable.

start.question: Will it be used mostly on phones?

then.question: Are there 3 to 5 main sections people switch between often?

then.why: The main sections stay one thumb tap away and always visible. Use icons with text labels.

then.question: Is there one main action, like Compose or Add?

then.why: One clear button for the most common action, in easy reach. Keep it to one action, not a menu of everything.
Fine for secondary links, but hidden menus get used less, so keep the most used sections visible on screen.

then.question: Is it a website people read, or an app people work in?
Hundreds of categories, like a big shop or news site?

then.why: Shows many categories at once in a grouped panel. Make it work with the keyboard and on click, not only on hover.
The standard most sites use, so people know it already. Keep it short so it does not eat small screens.

then.question: More than 7 places to go, or nested sections?

then.why: Room for many sections and nesting. Let it collapse on smaller screens, and add a command palette for power users.
A slim bar for 3 to 7 destinations that leaves room for the work. Always show labels.

decisions.title: Spinner, skeleton, progress bar or last known value?

start.question: Is there already data on screen from before, like numbers on a dashboard or an inbox list?

then.why: Leave the old data on screen with a small "Updating" note and when it was last updated, then change the values in place without moving anything. People keep reading the whole time, and a wait that keeps you busy feels shorter than an empty one. Only the very first load, when there is nothing to show yet, needs a skeleton.

then.question: Does it usually finish in under about one second?

then.why: Under a second, a loader only flashes and distracts. Respond to the click at once, for example with a pressed state or an optimistic update.

then.question: Can you tell how far along it is, like a percentage, steps or file size?

then.why: Real progress makes waiting easier and tells people whether to wait. Show steps or time left for long jobs, and let them cancel.

then.question: Are you loading a page or list whose layout you already know?

then.why: Grey shapes in the final layout make the page feel faster and stop it jumping when content arrives. A common rule of thumb: wait about 300 ms before showing it, and once shown keep it about 500 ms, so fast loads never flash.

Fine for short, unknown waits on one action. Wait about 300 ms before showing it so fast actions never flash (a rule of thumb). If it can take more than about 10 seconds, switch to a progress message and let people cancel.
Asking "Are you sure?" for every action trains people to click Yes without reading. Act at once and show a toast with Undo.

then.question: Is the loss big, like deleting an account, paying, or sending to many people?

then.use: Confirm dialog that names the thing
then.why: Say exactly what will happen ("Delete Northwind and its 24 files?") and label the button with the action, not OK. For the biggest losses, ask them to type the name.
For small losses a confirm step only slows people down. Act at once and let them undo.

decisions.title: When should a form show errors?

start.question: Is the field hard to get right the first time, like a new password or a username that may be taken?

then.use: Show progress as they type, errors after they leave
then.why: Tick the rules off as they are met instead of showing errors while people are still typing. Show a real error only once they move on. Source: Baymard on inline validation (2024).

then.question: Is the person submitting the whole form right now?

then.use: Error summary on top plus a message at each field
then.why: List every problem at the top, link each one to its field and move focus there; keep the message next to each field too. Source: GOV.UK Design System.

then.use: Check each field when they leave it
then.why: Wait until the person moves on, then say what is wrong, and clear the message on the keystroke that fixes it. The research is mixed: a 2009 test (Wroblewski) favoured checking after each field, a 2007 study (Bargas-Avila et al.) favoured the end of the form. Test with your own users.

start.question: Does the change apply at once, with no Save button?

then.why: A switch is an instant on or off, like a light switch. Never put switches in a form that waits for Save. Source: NN/g on toggle switches (2018).

then.question: Is it a single yes or no inside a form that gets submitted?

then.why: Use it for one yes or no that applies when the form is sent, like "Email me the receipt". Word it so that ticked means yes. Source: NN/g on checkboxes and radio buttons (2004).

then.question: Can people pick more than one option?

then.why: Each option is independent, like filters, so show them all and let people tick any number. Source: NN/g (2004).
Exactly one choice from a short list. Show every option, and preselect one or offer an explicit "None". Source: NN/g (2004).

start.question: Could you ask a simpler question that needs fewer options?

then.why: Fewer options beat any control. Rewrite the question, split it, or use what you already know about the person.

then.question: Do people already know their answer, like their country, city or company?

then.why: Let people type and pick from matches. It handles long lists that a dropdown makes painful.

then.question: Do all the options fit on screen?

then.why: Every choice is visible at once, easy to compare and easy to tap. Source: NN/g (2004).

Only for a medium list people browse when space is tight. In GOV.UK testing people struggled to close dropdowns, tried to type in them and missed that they scroll. No study gives a reliable option count to switch at.

decisions.title: Filters: update live or use an Apply button?

start.question: Is this a filter sheet on a phone?

then.why: On phones, let people set several filters in the sheet and apply once, so the page does not reload under their thumb. Source: NN/g on applying filters (2016).

then.question: Do results update almost instantly, well under a second?
Are people exploring rather than knowing exactly what they want?

then.why: Instant results let people see what each filter does and explore. Dim the results briefly while they update. Source: NN/g (2016).
When people know several criteria up front, one Apply saves them from watching the page reload after every tick. Source: NN/g (2016).
When results take a while, live filters freeze the page between every tick. Let people set them all, then apply once. Source: NN/g (2016).

decisions.title: Toast, inline message, banner or dialog?

start.question: Is it an error the person has to fix?

then.why: Put it next to the field or button it is about and keep it until it is fixed. Never a toast for errors. Sources: NN/g (2024); WCAG 2.2 Status Messages.

then.question: Does it block progress or need a decision?

then.why: Stop the page on purpose for a decision, with buttons named after the action. Return focus to where the person was when it closes.

then.question: Is it about the whole page or app, like being offline or a trial ending?

then.why: A bar at the top that stays until the situation changes, with what to do next.

Fine for a small confirmation of something the person just did, ideally with Undo. Keep it on screen long enough to read, announce it as a status, and make the result findable elsewhere. Source: Adrian Roselli on toast messages.

checks.check: Main buttons are big (at least 44 by 44 px on touch) and close to where the hand or pointer already is.
Each screen offers a few clear choices; rare options are tucked away.
Navigation, search, cart and forms work the way people know from other sites.
Long numbers, codes and lists are broken into small groups.
Related things are grouped by space or a shared box, and unrelated things sit apart.
Only one thing per screen stands out: the main action.
Hard parts are handled by smart defaults instead of being pushed onto the user.
People can always see what is happening, undo mistakes, and read words they use themselves.
Every action responds within about 400 ms, or shows feedback at once while it works.
Anything slower than a second shows progress.
Screens that already show data keep showing it while they refresh, with the time of the last update.
Error messages say what went wrong and how to fix it, in plain words.
Forms check fields as people go, not only after Submit.
Empty screens explain what goes there and offer the first step.
No dark patterns: no pre-ticked boxes, hidden costs or guilt-trip wording.
A failed submit lists every error at the top, with links to the fields.
Field labels stay visible above the fields, not only as placeholders.
Clicking Pay or Submit twice cannot create two orders.
Nothing on the page jumps as images, ads or banners load.
Body text contrast is at least 4.5:1, and the page still works at 200% zoom.
Real buttons, links and labels are used, and icon-only buttons have a name.
Every control shows a clear focus ring when using the keyboard.
Color is never the only signal; status also has text or an icon.
Animation calms down or stops when the system asks for reduced motion.
Motion is short and eases out when things enter.
Transitions show where content came from and went.

screens.label: Pricing
screens.what: A pricing card: plan name, monthly price, three included features and an Upgrade button.

screens.label: Landing
screens.what: A landing page top: a navbar with logo, links and Sign up, then a hero with a headline, one line of copy, a primary Start free button and a secondary See demo button.

screens.label: Product card
screens.what: A product card: image, name, price, a short detail line and an Add to cart button.

screens.label: Paywall
screens.what: An honest upgrade screen: plan name, a headline, three benefits, the price after the free trial with "Cancel anytime", a Not now button and a Start free trial button. No fake timers or guilt wording.

screens.label: Cookie consent
screens.what: A cookie consent panel: one line of why, Necessary (always on), switches for Analytics and Marketing (off by default), and Reject all and Accept all buttons of equal weight.

screens.label: Dashboard
screens.what: A dashboard: two stat tiles (revenue and orders, each with a short trend line), and a weekly sales bar chart with an Export button.

screens.label: Inbox
screens.what: An inbox: a header with Compose, then message rows with initials avatar, sender, subject preview and time. Unread rows are bold with a dot (not colour alone), and one row is selected.

screens.label: Editor
screens.what: A document editor: a formatting toolbar (bold, italic, list, link, undo, each with an accessible name), a title, an editable text area, a word count with save status and a Publish button.

screens.label: Data table
screens.what: A data table of invoices: number, customer, status written as text (Paid, Due, Overdue) and amount, with Previous and Next paging.

screens.label: Settings
screens.what: A settings panel: a heading, three labelled switches, and Cancel and Save buttons.

screens.label: Dialog
screens.what: A confirm dialog over a dimmed page: a question naming the thing, one line on what happens, Cancel and Delete.

screens.label: Chat
screens.what: A chat: a header with the person and their status, message bubbles from both sides, and a message field with Send.

screens.label: Sign in
screens.what: A sign in form: email and password fields with labels, a Forgot password link and a Sign in button.

screens.label: Google / Apple sign in
screens.what: A create account screen: Continue with Google and Continue with Apple buttons (text labels), an "or" divider, an email field and Continue with email.

screens.label: Onboarding
screens.what: An onboarding step: a picture area, "Step 2 of 3" in text, a title, one line of benefit, step dots, and Skip and Next.

screens.label: Feed post
screens.what: A social feed post: author avatar, name and time, a short caption, an image, and like, comment and share buttons with counts.

screens.label: Search
screens.what: Search results: a search field with a Search button, filter toggles (pressed state visible), and result rows with name, price and a short detail.

screens.label: Profile
screens.what: A profile: large initials avatar, name and handle, three stats (orders, reviews, rating), and Edit profile and Share buttons.

screens.label: Checkout
screens.what: A checkout summary: two line items with prices, delivery, the total, the payment method with Change, and a Pay button showing the amount.

screens.label: Empty state
screens.what: An empty state: a simple outline icon, "No projects yet", one line on what goes here, a Create project button and a secondary Import option.

screens.label: Notification prompt
screens.what: A notification permission prompt shown before the system one: an icon, the question, one honest line on what they will get, and Not now and Allow.
